methods.title: Checking Normality (range percentages, Q-Q plot, Shapiro-Wilk)
methods.trigger: A question asks whether data are Normally distributed, shows qqnorm or shapiro.test output, or asks whether a parametric test is appropriate.

methods.title: Mann-Whitney rank-sum test with the T table (n_B at most 8)
methods.trigger: Two groups of different individuals, ordinal or non-Normal data, and the bigger group has 8 or fewer observations.

methods.title: Mann-Whitney with the Normal approximation and ties (n_B > 8)
methods.trigger: Two groups of different individuals with non-Normal or skewed data and more than 8 observations in the bigger group.

methods.title: Wilcoxon signed-rank test with the W table (n at most 8)
methods.trigger: The same subjects are measured twice (before and after), the differences are ordinal or non-Normal, and there are 8 or fewer nonzero differences.

methods.title: Wilcoxon signed-rank with the Normal approximation and ties (n > 8)
methods.trigger: Before-and-after data on the same subjects with more than 8 nonzero differences, often with tied magnitudes.

cases.title: Checking Normality of two ten-value samples
cases.context: Two samples of ten values are checked for Normality with range percentages, qqnorm() and shapiro.test(). Sample 2 equals sample 1 except that 60 is replaced by 50 and 68 by 88.
tasks: For each sample, calculate the mean, the SD, and the percentage of values within one SD of the mean, and compare it with the Normal percentage.
Give the theoretical quantiles that qqnorm() uses for ten points.
Using the shapiro.test output, state the hypotheses, the decision at the 0.05 level, and what it says about using a parametric test.

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{the data come from a Normal distribution}
hypotheses.alternative: H_A:\text{the data do not come from a Normal distribution}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference between the distribution of the data and a Normal distribution.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The distribution of the data differs from a Normal distribution.

cases.symbols: \(\bar x\) (sample mean), \(s\) (sample SD), \(p_i\) (plotting probability), \(z_i\) (theoretical Normal quantile), \(W\) (Shapiro-Wilk statistic), \(P\) (P value).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
general: H_0:\text{the data come from a Normal distribution}
H_A:\text{the data do not come from a Normal distribution}
steps.words: Normality is checked with the percentage of data in a range, the Normal Q-Q plot, and the Shapiro-Wilk test. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference between the distribution of the data and a Normal distribution.

steps.title: Mean and SD of sample 1
steps.words: Add the ten values and divide by 10, then square each deviation, add them, divide by n - 1 = 9 and take the root.

steps.title: Percentage of sample 1 within one SD
steps.words: Seven of the ten values (62, 62, 63, 64, 64, 65, 65) lie within one SD of the mean. This 70% is close to the Normal 68.26%, and all ten values lie within two SDs, close to the Normal 95.44%.

steps.title: Theoretical quantiles for qqnorm()
steps.words: For ten or fewer points R uses these plotting probabilities. The ten theoretical quantiles run from -1.54664 to +1.54664 and are the horizontal axis of the Q-Q plot. Sample 1 plotted against them lies close to a straight line.

steps.title: Shapiro-Wilk result for sample 1
steps.words: The P value is far above 0.05, so Normality is not rejected. The data are consistent with a Normal distribution, and a parametric test can be used.

steps.title: Mean, SD and range percentages of sample 2
steps.words: The two extreme values inflate the SD, so eight values crowd inside one SD (80% against 68.26%) while 88 lies beyond two SDs (90% within two SDs against 95.44%). The counts depart from the Normal percentages.

steps.title: Shapiro-Wilk result for sample 2
steps.words: The P value is below 0.05 (and below 0.01), so Normality is rejected. The Q-Q plot shows 50 and 88 far from the line through the other points, and a rank-based test is preferred for these data.

cases.conclusion: Sample 1 gives W = 0.97577 with P = 0.9386, so Normality is not rejected and the data are consistent with a Normal distribution. Sample 2 gives W = 0.75726 with P = 0.004374, so Normality is rejected and the data are not Normal.

cases.title: Diuretic experiment with three placebo and four drug values
cases.context: Daily urine production is measured in three people given a placebo and four different people given a drug. The data are ranked to test whether the drug changes urine production without assuming Normal populations.
tasks: Rank all seven observations together and compute T for the smaller group.
Use the printed T table to test at the level near 0.05 whether the drug changes urine production. State the hypotheses in words and the conclusion.

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{same distribution of urine production with placebo and drug}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in the distributions of daily urine production between the placebo and drug groups, so the drug has no effect.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The distributions of daily urine production differ between the placebo and drug groups.

cases.symbols: \(T\) (sum of ranks in the smaller group), \(n_S\) (size of the smaller group), \(n_B\) (size of the bigger group), \(\mu_T\) (mean of \(T\) under the null hypothesis), \(\sigma_T\) (standard deviation of \(T\) under the null hypothesis), \(z_T\) (standardized rank sum).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
general: H_0:\text{the two population distributions are the same}
steps.words: The groups contain different people and the bigger group has 4 people, so the procedure is the Mann-Whitney rank-sum test with the T table. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in the distributions of daily urine production between placebo and drug.

steps.title: Rank all observations together
steps.words: All seven values are ranked in one list regardless of group. There are no ties.

steps.title: Compute T
steps.words: The placebo group is the smaller group, so T is the sum of its three ranks.

steps.title: Describe the null distribution of T
steps.words: Under the null hypothesis each of the 35 sets of three ranks is equally likely. The rank sums run from 6 to 18 and are centered at 12.

steps.title: Read the critical values
steps.words: Open MannWhitney_RankSumT_Table.pdf, PDF page 1. In the row n_S = 3, n_B = 4 under probability levels near .05, the printed critical values are 6 and 18 with P = .057. No .01 entry is printed for this row.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: T = 9 lies strictly between 6 and 18, so the null hypothesis is not rejected. Fourteen of the 35 rank sets are at least as far from 12 as T = 9, so the exact two-tailed P is 0.4.

cases.conclusion: T = 9 lies between the critical values 6 and 18, so the null hypothesis is not rejected (P = 0.4). These data do not show that the drug changes daily urine production.

cases.title: Leboyer versus control delivery, minutes of alert behavior
cases.context: Twenty infants delivered by conventional gentle techniques (control) and twenty delivered by the Leboyer method have their minutes of alert behavior recorded during the first hour of life. The times are skewed toward higher values.
tasks: Rank all 40 times together and compute T.
Use the Normal approximation to test at the two-sided 0.05 level whether the distributions differ. Give the mean and SD of T, z_T, the printed critical value, the decision and a P range.

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{same distribution of alert minutes for control and Leboyer}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in the distributions of the number of minutes awake in the first hour after birth between the two birth-method groups.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The distributions of minutes awake in the first hour differ between the two birth-method groups.

cases.symbols: \(T\) (sum of ranks in the smaller group), \(n_S\) (size of the smaller group), \(n_B\) (size of the bigger group), \(\mu_T\) (mean of \(T\) under the null hypothesis), \(\sigma_T\) (standard deviation of \(T\) under the null hypothesis), \(z_T\) (standardized rank sum).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
general: H_0:\text{the two population distributions are the same}
steps.words: The two groups contain different infants and the times are skewed, so the procedure is the Mann-Whitney rank-sum test. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in the distributions of minutes awake in the first hour after birth between the two birth-method groups.

steps.title: Rank all 40 times and compute T
steps.words: No two times are equal, so every rank is a whole number. The groups have equal size, and the control group is used as on the slide.

steps.title: Choose the Normal approximation
steps.words: The bigger group has more than 8 observations, so the T table does not apply and T is treated as Normal.

steps.title: Mean of T
steps.words: This is the rank sum expected for the control group if the method has no effect.

steps.title: Standard deviation of T
steps.words: There are no ties, so the simple form of the standard deviation applies.

steps.title: Compute z_T
steps.words: The continuity correction subtracts one half from the distance between T and its mean before dividing by the standard deviation.

steps.title: Read the critical value
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 2. In the infinity row and the two-tailed 0.05 column, the printed value is 1.9600.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: The statistic is below 1.96, so the null hypothesis is not rejected. In the infinity row it lies between the 0.50 and 0.20 columns, so 0.20 < P < 0.50.

cases.conclusion: T = 374 gives z_T = 0.960278, which is less than 1.9600, so the null hypothesis is not rejected (0.20 < P < 0.50). The data do not show a difference in minutes of alert behavior between Leboyer and control deliveries.

cases.title: Potential diuretic in six people, before and after
cases.context: Six people have daily urine production measured before and after taking a potential diuretic. The signed-rank test is used without assuming Normal differences.
tasks: Compute the differences, rank their magnitudes, attach the signs and compute W.
Use the printed W table to test whether the drug changes urine production. State the hypotheses in words and the conclusion.

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{no difference in urine production before and after the drug}
hypotheses.alternative: H_A:\text{urine production differs before and after the drug}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in daily urine production before and after the drug, so the drug has no effect.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Daily urine production differs before and after the drug.

cases.symbols: \(W\) (sum of the signed ranks), \(n\) (number of nonzero differences), \(\mu_W\) (mean of \(W\) under the null hypothesis), \(\sigma_W\) (standard deviation of \(W\) under the null hypothesis), \(z_W\) (standardized signed-rank sum).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: Each person is measured before and after, so the procedure is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and with 6 nonzero differences the W table is used. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in daily urine production before and after the drug.

steps.title: Compute the differences
steps.words: No difference is zero, so all six people are kept.

steps.title: Rank the magnitudes and attach signs
steps.words: The smallest magnitude, 10, gets rank 1 and the largest, 550, gets rank 6. Each rank then takes the sign of its difference.

steps.title: Compute W
steps.words: The positive rank is 4 and the negative ranks add to 17.

steps.title: Read the critical value
steps.words: Open WilcoxonW_Table.pdf, PDF page 1, row n = 6. The printed critical values are 21 with P = .032 and 19 with P = .062. The value 21 is the one whose P does not exceed 0.05.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: The magnitude 13 is below both printed critical values, so the null hypothesis is not rejected. Fourteen of the 64 equally likely sign patterns give |W| of 13 or more.

cases.conclusion: W = -13 and |W| = 13 is below the critical value of 21 (and below 19), so the null hypothesis is not rejected (P = 0.219). The data do not show that the drug changes daily urine production.

cases.title: Lecture exercise, platelet aggregation with the signed-rank test
cases.context: Eleven people have maximum percentage platelet aggregation measured before and after smoking one cigarette. The Session 24 lecture exercise analyzes the same data used for the paired t test with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
tasks: Rank the magnitudes of the differences with average ranks for ties, attach the signs and compute W.
Use the tie-corrected Normal approximation to test at the two-sided 0.05 level. Give sigma_W, z_W, the printed critical value, the decision and the P range, and compare with the paired t test.

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{no difference in platelet aggregation before and after smoking}
hypotheses.alternative: H_A:\text{platelet aggregation differs before and after smoking}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in platelet aggregation before and after smoking a single cigarette.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Platelet aggregation differs before and after smoking a single cigarette.

cases.symbols: \(W\) (sum of the signed ranks), \(n\) (number of nonzero differences), \(\mu_W\) (mean of \(W\) under the null hypothesis), \(\sigma_W\) (standard deviation of \(W\) under the null hypothesis), \(z_W\) (standardized signed-rank sum). \(\tau_i\) (number of tied ranks in the \(i\)th set of ties).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: The same people are measured before and after, so the procedure is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and with 11 nonzero differences the Normal approximation is used. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in platelet aggregation before and after smoking a single cigarette.

steps.title: Compute the differences
steps.words: No difference is zero, so n stays 11.

steps.title: Rank the magnitudes with ties
general: \text{tied rank}=\text{average of the ranks the tied values occupy}
steps.words: The magnitudes 4 and 4 share ranks 3 and 4, and the magnitudes 15 and 15 share ranks 8 and 9. The change of -1 has the smallest magnitude and gets rank 1.

steps.title: Compute W
steps.words: Only the rank of the -1 change is negative, so W is the total of all ranks, 66, minus twice 1.

steps.title: Tie sum
steps.words: There are two sets of ties, each of size 2.

steps.title: Tie-corrected standard deviation of W
steps.words: The ties reduce the variance by 1, from 506 to 505.

steps.title: Compute z_W
steps.words: The mean of W under the null hypothesis is zero, so only the continuity correction is subtracted from |W|.

steps.title: Read the critical value
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 2. In the infinity row and the two-tailed 0.05 column, the printed value is 1.9600.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: The statistic exceeds 1.96, so the null hypothesis is rejected. In the infinity row it passes the 0.005 column (2.8070) but not the 0.002 column (3.0902), so 0.002 < P < 0.005. The paired t test on page 26 also rejects, with t = 4.27 and P < 0.002.

cases.conclusion: W = 64 and z_W = 2.82571 exceeds 1.9600, so the null hypothesis is rejected (0.002 < P < 0.005). Smoking one cigarette increases platelet aggregation, in agreement with the paired t test.
cases.source: Session 24 page 27 (lecture exercise), data and paired t test on page 26

cases.title: Original practice example, days to normal walking under two protocols
cases.context: Original practice example with invented illustrative data. Four people follow rehabilitation protocol A and six different people follow protocol B, and the number of days until normal walking is recorded.
tasks: Rank all ten observations together, using average ranks for ties, and compute T.
Use the printed T table to test whether the protocols differ. State the hypotheses in words, the decision and a P range.

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{same distribution of days to normal walking for A and B}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in the distributions of days to normal walking between protocols A and B.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The distributions of days to normal walking differ between protocols A and B.

cases.symbols: \(T\) (sum of ranks in the smaller group), \(n_S\) (size of the smaller group), \(n_B\) (size of the bigger group), \(\mu_T\) (mean of \(T\) under the null hypothesis), \(\sigma_T\) (standard deviation of \(T\) under the null hypothesis), \(z_T\) (standardized rank sum).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
general: H_0:\text{the two population distributions are the same}
steps.words: The groups contain different people and the bigger group has 6 people, so the procedure is the Mann-Whitney rank-sum test with the T table. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in the distributions of days to normal walking between the protocols.

steps.title: Rank all observations with ties
general: \text{tied rank}=\text{average of the ranks the tied values occupy}
steps.words: The two values of 10 would occupy ranks 6 and 7, so each receives 6.5.

steps.title: Compute T
steps.words: Protocol A is the smaller group.

steps.title: Read the critical values
steps.words: Open MannWhitney_RankSumT_Table.pdf, PDF page 1, row n_S = 4, n_B = 6. Near .05 the printed critical values are 12 and 32 with P = .038, and near .01 they are 10 and 34 with P = .010.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: T = 11 is at or below the lower value 12, so the null hypothesis is rejected. It does not reach the .01 lower value of 10, so 0.010 < P < 0.038.

cases.conclusion: T = 11 is at or below the lower critical value of 12, so the null hypothesis is rejected (0.010 < P < 0.038). Protocol A tends to give fewer days to normal walking than protocol B.

cases.title: Original practice example, grip strength before and after hand therapy
cases.context: Original practice example with invented illustrative data. Nine people have grip strength measured before and after a hand-therapy program, and one person shows no change.
tasks: Drop the zero difference, rank the magnitudes with average ranks for ties, attach the signs and compute W.
Use the printed W table to test whether grip strength changes. State the hypotheses in words, the decision and a P range.

hypotheses.null: H_0:\text{no difference in grip strength before and after therapy}
hypotheses.alternative: H_A:\text{grip strength differs before and after therapy}
hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference in grip strength before and after the hand-therapy program.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Grip strength differs before and after the hand-therapy program.

cases.symbols: \(W\) (sum of the signed ranks), \(n\) (number of nonzero differences), \(\mu_W\) (mean of \(W\) under the null hypothesis), \(\sigma_W\) (standard deviation of \(W\) under the null hypothesis), \(z_W\) (standardized signed-rank sum).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: Each person is measured before and after, so the procedure is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in grip strength before and after the program.

steps.title: Drop the zero difference
steps.words: Person 3 has no change, so that difference is dropped and n becomes 8. The W table applies.

steps.title: Rank the magnitudes and attach signs
steps.words: The two magnitudes of 3 share ranks 2 and 3. Only the -1 change has a negative sign.

steps.title: Compute W
steps.words: The positive ranks add to 35 and the single negative rank is 1.

steps.title: Read the critical value
steps.words: Open WilcoxonW_Table.pdf, PDF page 1, row n = 8. The printed critical values are 32 with P = .024 and 28 with P = .054. The value 32 is the one whose P does not exceed 0.05.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: The magnitude 34 reaches the critical value of 32, so the null hypothesis is rejected. It is beyond the largest printed critical value for n = 8, so P < 0.024.

cases.conclusion: W = 34 with n = 8 reaches the critical value of 32, so the null hypothesis is rejected (P < 0.024). Grip strength increases after the hand-therapy program.

sampleQuestions.stem: What is the null hypothesis of the Shapiro-Wilk test?
options: The data are not Normally distributed.
The two group means are equal.
sampleQuestions.why: The test compares the distribution of the data with the Normal distribution, and the null hypothesis is that there is no difference between them.

sampleQuestions.stem: A Shapiro-Wilk test gives P = 0.9386. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The data are proven to come from a Normal distribution.
Normality is not rejected, so the data are consistent with a Normal distribution.
The data are not Normal because P is large.
A rank test must be used.
sampleQuestions.why: A large P value means the data give no evidence against Normality. Failing to reject does not prove the null hypothesis.

sampleQuestions.stem: On a Normal Q-Q plot the middle points follow the line, but the largest points rise far above it and the smallest fall far below it. Which shape does this show?
sampleQuestions.why: Extreme values that are more extreme than Normal quantiles predict at both ends are the heavy-tail pattern on page 7.

sampleQuestions.stem: On a Normal Q-Q plot the points bend upward away from the line only at the right end. Which shape does this show?
sampleQuestions.why: The largest values are larger than Normal quantiles predict, which is the positive-skew pattern with a long right tail.

sampleQuestions.stem: For sample 1 on page 8 (60, 62, 62, 63, 64, 64, 65, 65, 67, 68), what is the sample SD?
sampleQuestions.why: The squared deviations add to 52. Dividing by n - 1 = 9 gives 5.77778, and its square root is 2.4037.

sampleQuestions.stem: For sample 1, what percentage of the values lies within one SD of the mean, and how does it compare with a Normal distribution?
sampleQuestions.why: The interval 61.596 to 66.404 contains 62, 62, 63, 64, 64, 65 and 65, which is 7 of 10 values. A Normal distribution has 68.26% within one SD.

sampleQuestions.stem: qqnorm() for ten points uses plotting probabilities (i - 3/8)/(n + 1/4). What is the theoretical quantile of the smallest point?
sampleQuestions.why: The plotting probability is (1 - 0.375)/10.25 = 0.0609756, and the standard Normal quantile at that probability is -1.54664.

sampleQuestions.stem: Sample 2 on page 8 gives W = 0.75726 and p-value = 0.004374 from shapiro.test. What is the correct decision at the 0.05 level?
options: Do not reject the null hypothesis, so the data are Normally distributed.
Reject the null hypothesis, so the data are not Normally distributed.
Reject the null hypothesis, so the two samples have different means.
No decision is possible without the T table.
sampleQuestions.why: The Shapiro-Wilk null hypothesis is Normality. A P value of 0.004374 is below 0.05, so Normality is rejected.
